title: How to Restore Deleted WhatsApp Chats Using Local Database msgstore.db.crypt14
metaTitle: Restore Deleted WhatsApp Chats from Local Database (2026)
metaDescription: Accidentally deleted critical WhatsApp messages with no Google Drive backup? Learn how to restore chats using local encrypted database backup files (msgstore.db.crypt14).

excerpt: When Google Drive cloud backups fail or overwrite your messages, Android still stores 7 days of daily local database snapshots. Here is how to restore them.
description: Step-by-step forensic guide on recovering deleted WhatsApp chats and media using local crypt14 and crypt15 database archives on internal Android storage without cloud backups.

faq.title: Where does WhatsApp store local database backups on Android 11, 12, 13, 14, and 15?
faq.description: Due to Google's Scoped Storage regulations, WhatsApp's local database directory moved from the root folder to: `Internal Storage/Android/media/com.whatsapp/WhatsApp/Databases/`. You can browse this folder using any standard file manager application like Google Files, Solid Explorer, or Mi File Manager.

faq.title: Can I read the contents of 'msgstore.db.crypt14' directly on my computer in Notepad?
faq.description: No. The file is protected by AES-256 bit symmetric cryptography. The cryptographic key required to decrypt the database (`key` file) is stored in the protected system partition `/data/data/com.whatsapp/files/key`, which is inaccessible without root privileges. To read the chats, the file must be restored through the official WhatsApp application using your verified phone number.

faq.title: Why does WhatsApp keep trying to restore from Google Drive instead of my local file?
faq.description: If your phone is logged into a Google Account that contains an existing Google Drive WhatsApp backup, the setup wizard will always prioritize the cloud backup over local storage. To force WhatsApp to restore from your renamed local `msgstore.db.crypt14` file, you must disconnect Google Drive backup permissions or turn off Wi-Fi/data during the initial restore detection prompt.

html:
The Devastating Accident of an Erased Chat Thread

It happens in a split second of inattention: you intend to tap 'Clear Chat' or swipe away a notification, but instead you inadvertently tap 'Delete Chat' on a conversation containing critical business agreements, legal evidence, cherished messages from a deceased family member, or important tax documents. To make matters worse, when you check Google Drive, you discover that your last cloud backup executed three weeks ago, or worse, that Google Drive just completed an automated scheduled sync 10 minutes after the deletion, permanently overwriting your cloud archive with the blank state.

Before you succumb to despair or pay exorbitant sums for predatory 'WhatsApp Spy Data Recovery' software online, understand this crucial architectural fact: Android stores a rolling 7-day archive of encrypted local database snapshots directly on your phone's internal storage. Every single morning at 2:00 AM, WhatsApp compiles an encrypted snapshot of your entire chat history into a file named msgstore.db.crypt14 (or crypt15). This comprehensive forensic tutorial walks you through locating, renaming, and restoring these local database files to recover your lost conversations without relying on Google Drive.

The Architecture of WhatsApp's Scoped Storage on Android

To recover your files, you must navigate Android's file system. Prior to Android 10, WhatsApp stored its databases in a simple root directory: /sdcard/WhatsApp/Databases/. However, beginning with Android 11 and enforced strictly in Android 13, 14, and 15, Google instituted Scoped Storage security guidelines to prevent rogue apps from reading each other's storage partitions.

Today, WhatsApp's local database repository is housed inside the sandboxed media directory:

Internal Storage > Android > media > com.whatsapp > WhatsApp > Databases

Inside this folder, you will observe several files formatted with specific naming conventions:

  • msgstore.db.crypt14 (The active, current live database representing your most recent chat state).
  • msgstore-2026-11-25.1.db.crypt14 (The daily rolling snapshot automatically created yesterday at 2:00 AM).
  • msgstore-2026-11-24.1.db.crypt14 (The snapshot created two days ago).
  • ...extending backward for exactly seven consecutive days.

By substituting the active live database with a dated snapshot created before the accidental deletion occurred, you can force WhatsApp to reconstruct your message history down to the exact second that snapshot was captured.

Prerequisites Before Starting Recovery

Before executing file operations, prepare these essential requirements:

  1. A Capable File Manager: While Google's default Files by Google app works, an advanced file manager like Solid Explorer, Mi File Manager, or Cx File Explorer allows you to view file extensions and rename system files much more reliably.
  2. Sufficient Free Storage: Ensure your phone has at least 2 GB of free internal storage. The restoration process temporarily extracts and indexes database indices.
  3. Your Registered SIM Card Active: You must be able to receive the 6-digit SMS verification code to re-authenticate your WhatsApp profile.

Step-by-Step Restoration Protocol

Step 1: Locate and Copy the Databases Directory (Safety Backup)

  1. Open your file manager application.
  2. Navigate to: Internal Storage > Android > media > com.whatsapp > WhatsApp.
  3. Locate the Databases folder.
  4. Long-press the Databases folder, select Copy, and paste a duplicate copy into your phone's Documents or Download folder. This guarantees that even if you make a typographical error during renaming, your raw historical snapshots remain 100% safe.

Step 2: Rename the Historical Target Database

  1. Inside the original .../WhatsApp/Databases/ folder, look at the dated files.
  2. Identify the file whose date corresponds to the day immediately prior to when your chats were deleted. For example, if you deleted your chat on November 26, look for: msgstore-2026-11-25.1.db.crypt14.
  3. If there is already a file named strictly msgstore.db.crypt14, rename it to msgstore-CORRUPT.db.crypt14 to get it out of the way.
  4. Now, select your target dated file (msgstore-2026-11-25.1.db.crypt14) and tap Rename.
  5. Carefully strip out the date string from the filename so it reads exactly:
    msgstore.db.crypt14
    (Caution: Do not alter the crypt extension number, whether it is crypt14 or crypt15).

Step 3: Disconnect Google Drive to Force Local Restoration

This is the critical step where 90% of users fail: if WhatsApp detects an active Google Drive backup, it will bypass your local storage file and pull the cloud backup instead.

  1. Open your web browser (or computer) and navigate to: https://drive.google.com.
  2. Sign in with the Google Account linked to your phone.
  3. Click the Gear icon (Settings) in the upper right > tap Settings > select Manage Apps.
  4. Scroll down to find WhatsApp Messenger.
  5. Click Options next to WhatsApp and select Disconnect from Drive. (Alternatively, on your phone: go to Settings > Accounts > Google and temporarily remove the Google Account, or simply turn on Airplane mode right after SMS verification).

Step 4: Reinstall and Trigger Local Database Restore

  1. Now, on your phone: long-press the WhatsApp app icon > tap App info > select Uninstall. (Do NOT check 'Keep app data' if prompted).
  2. Open the Google Play Store and reinstall WhatsApp Messenger.
  3. Launch WhatsApp, select your language, and tap Agree and Continue.
  4. Enter your mobile phone number and verify the 6-digit SMS OTP.
  5. Grant the mandatory permissions for Contacts and Storage / Photos and Videos. (Granting storage access is mandatory so WhatsApp can scan the /Android/media/com.whatsapp/ folder).
  6. WhatsApp will initialize its local scanner. Because Google Drive is disconnected, the screen will display: 'Backup found (Local Backup)', showing the date and size of your renamed msgstore.db.crypt14 file!
  7. Tap the green Restore button. Do NOT tap 'Skip'.
  8. Wait while the progress bar restores your messages. Once completed, tap Next. Your complete chat threads, contacts, and media linkages from that snapshot date will appear on your home screen.

Troubleshooting Restoration Errors

Encountered Issue Root Technical Cause Corrective Action
WhatsApp says 'No backup found' after reinstall WhatsApp installed from wrong package or permissions not granted Ensure storage permission is granted; verify the file is named strictly msgstore.db.crypt14
Only messages from 2 years ago restore WhatsApp connected to an ancient Google Drive cloud file Disconnect WhatsApp from Google Drive settings; clear WhatsApp data; re-trigger restore
Restore progress bar stuck at 24% or 99% Corrupted SQLite table or low internal storage headroom Ensure >2GB free storage; try the snapshot from two days prior (e.g., msgstore-2026-11-24)
Photos appear as blurry question marks Database restored successfully, but media folder was wiped Media is stored in /WhatsApp/Media; check if media files still exist in file manager

Database Forensics: Understanding Crypt14 and Crypt15 Encryption

WhatsApp's local backups are not plain text SQLite databases; they are encrypted archives protected by AES-GCM-256 bit authenticated encryption:

  • The Header Structure: The first 67 bytes of every crypt14 file contain initialization vectors, protocol buffer version tokens, and key derivation metadata. Altering these header bytes corrupts the entire SQLite payload beyond salvage.
  • The Cryptographic Key: When WhatsApp generates a backup, it requests the master symmetric key stored inside /data/data/com.whatsapp/files/key. This key is derived during initial SMS verification and never leaves the smartphone unless End-to-End Encrypted Cloud Backups are explicitly enabled.
  • The Inode Integrity: Because the local file system writes sequential WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) checkpoints, if your phone suddenly powers off during the 2:00 AM backup creation, WhatsApp preserves the previous day's database intact. That is why having the rolling 7-day history is an indispensable safeguard against unexpected database corruption.

Handling Voice Notes, Photos, and Media Folders After Restoration

A frequent complication after restoring a local msgstore.db.crypt14 file is that message bubbles display properly, but voice notes, videos, and images appear with blurred thumbnails or question marks when tapped. This occurs because the SQLite database stores the metadata pointer (the file path and encryption hash), whereas the actual binary payload resides in the file system:

  • Media Storage Directory: Navigate to Internal Storage > Android > media > com.whatsapp > WhatsApp > Media.
  • Inside this folder, you will find subdirectories: WhatsApp Audio, WhatsApp Images, WhatsApp Video, and WhatsApp Voice Notes.
  • Preventing Automated Deletion: Never delete the Media folder during an app uninstall. If you manually reinstall WhatsApp, ensure that the file manager path remains intact before you complete phone number verification. If the media files remain in their respective subdirectories, WhatsApp will instantly re-link the cryptographic hashes to the restored chat bubbles, allowing you to listen to voice notes and view images seamlessly.

Dealing with Corrupted Local SQLite Headers

In rare instances where a phone battery died precisely during the automated 2:00 AM backup routine, the latest dated msgstore.db.crypt14 may suffer from truncated database headers. When WhatsApp attempts to restore a corrupted file, the progress dialog freezes at 24% or 99% before aborting with an error.

To resolve this, return to your /Databases directory and inspect file sizes. Healthy WhatsApp backups usually maintain a consistent file size (e.g., 42 MB, 43 MB, 44 MB). If the most recent file is suspiciously small (e.g., 8 MB or 12 MB), it was interrupted mid-write. Simply delete that broken file and choose the snapshot from two days prior (such as msgstore-2026-11-24.1.db.crypt14). Renaming this older, intact snapshot guarantees a smooth, 100% completion rate without database freeze errors.

Charging Wattage Curvature & Thermal Stepping Mechanics

Many smartphone buyers believe that an '80W' or '120W' phone charges at that maximum wattage continuously from 0% to 100%. In reality, battery charging follows a strict algorithmic curve dictated by electrochemical safety limits:

  • Phase 1: Peak Pulse (0% to 25%): The charging IC allows maximum rated power (e.g., 100W at 9.2A). Temperatures rise at a steep rate of 1.2°C per minute.
  • Phase 2: First Thermal Step-Down (25% to 65%): As battery voltage crosses 4.1V and internal temperature hits 39°C, the power management chip aggressively drops wattage to 45W to 55W to prevent thermal runaway.
  • Phase 3: Constant Voltage Saturation (65% to 100%): Current steadily tapers down from 30W to 12W, and finally drops to a trickle 4W above 90%.

If your room ambient temperature exceeds 32°C (common across Indian summer months), the phone will trigger Phase 2 thermal step-down almost immediately at 15% charge. Placing your smartphone in front of a gentle desk fan or charging in an air-conditioned room keeps the device beneath the 38°C threshold, allowing high-wattage charging to persist without heating the motherboard.

Preventative Architecture & Companion Recommendations

Local database restoration is an indispensable safety net, but proactive multi-layer backup architecture ensures you never face panic again.
